rv.q: In this pure, funny, beautifully bittersweet Goodman production of Chekhov's last play, the source of humor is well-pinpointed in humans' fundamental inability to change.
It's not only a tautly adapted and directed play, but a masterclass in acting.
You won’t be quick to forget this epic night at the theatre.

Falls has molded Chekov’s vision of the collapse of mid-19th century servitude society into an assessable production that looks and feels very much like it might have at the Moscow Art Theater during its debut at turn of the 20th century.
THE CHERRY ORCHARD is a perfect farewell for Robert Falls’ long reign as Artistic Director.
The director and his troupe hit every mark in a dazzling theatrical feat.

Filled with memorable characters, pathos, lots of humor and many haunting beats, this show will be remembered as a production that Anton Chekhov, himself, would have undoubtedly given a standing ovation.

Falls’ take on the play will likely endure, too, and predicts new beginnings for the director.
Falls captures that moment of change in all of its confusion and pain while keeping one eye on what makes the past nostalgic and romantic.

Fry brings a lovely wistfulness to Renevskaya's sense of connection to the home and orchard, and to the privileged life she is losing. But a more intense sense of loss (and even bitterness) is needed to anchor this play.
If one had to choose a perfect ending for Robert Falls’ three-decade career as Artistic Director at the Goodman Theatre, his production of "The Cherry Orchard" would be it.
The Cherry Orchard is very entertaining and a comedic joy to watch.
If you are one that hated to see his plays, you might find a whole new perspective and a love for the thoughts and ideas of this wonderful writer.

cn.t: Robert Falls' adaptation of Chekhov's classic serves as a triumphant farewell to his Goodman Theatre tenure, with critics praising its surprisingly comedic tone and masterful direction that balances humor with profound emotional depth.
